title: 1 Kings 1:41–53
context: Adonijah and all the guests who were with him hear the noise as they finish eating. When Joab hears the trumpet, he asks, “Why is this noise of the city being in an uproar?” While he is still speaking, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest arrives, and Adonijah welcomes him as a worthy man who brings good news. Jonathan answers that David has made Solomon king. He reports the mule, the escort of Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, the anointing at Gihon, the city’s ringing joy, Solomon sitting on the throne of the kingdom, the servants’ blessing on David, David’s bow on the bed, and David’s own word: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has given one to sit on my throne today, my eyes even seeing it.” The guests are afraid and go their way. Adonijah, afraid because of Solomon, goes and hangs onto the horns of the altar, asking that Solomon first swear not to kill him with the sword. Solomon answers with a condition: “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of his shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.” Solomon has him brought down from the altar; Adonijah bows, and Solomon says, “Go to your house.” Both traditions describe this as conditional clemency, not as a final clearing of whatever Adonijah may yet do, and they do not treat the horns of the altar as a cue for typology.

verses.text: Adonijah and all the guests who were with him heard it as they had finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, “Why is this noise of the city being in an uproar?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Adonijah and his guests hear the sound “as they had finished eating.” Joab, hearing the trumpet, asks, “Why is this noise of the city being in an uproar?” The feast has ended, and the city’s noise reaches the men who were not called to Gihon.

Arminian readers hear the two gatherings now colliding in real time. Joab’s question is honest alarm, not yet a report of what has happened.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the uproar as the sound already described, now heard at En Rogel. The trumpet Joab hears is the trumpet blown for Solomon.

Both traditions set the scene without ridicule. The claimant and his captain are still at table’s end when the city rises.

verses.text: While he yet spoke, behold, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came; and Adonijah said, “Come in; for you are a worthy man, and bring good news.”
verses.arminianNotes:
While Joab is still speaking, Jonathan the son of Abiathar the priest came, and Adonijah says, “Come in; for you are a worthy man, and bring good news.” Adonijah expects a welcome report from a man he trusts.

Arminian readers hear a real misjudgment. Adonijah’s confidence that the news is good is his own, and it will not be borne out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the irony without embellishing it. A worthy man does come, and he does bring news, but it is not the news Adonijah named as good.

Both traditions keep the verse as a greeting and an expectation, and they let the next speech supply the content.

verses.text: Jonathan answered Adonijah, “Most certainly our lord King David has made Solomon king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan answers, “Most certainly our lord King David has made Solomon king”. The speech that follows, through verse 48, is his report. The first word is not rumor but David’s act.

Arminian readers hear a clear statement of fact. Solomon is king because David has made him king, not because Jonathan has chosen him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also place the weight on David’s deed. “Most certainly” introduces a report of what the king has done.

Both traditions take this opening line as the turning of the feast: the succession has already been settled by David.

verses.text: The king has sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and they have caused him to ride on the king’s mule.
verses.arminianNotes:
He names the escort: the king has sent Zadok, Nathan, Benaiah, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, “and they have caused him to ride on the king’s mule.” The signs David commanded are described as already done.

Arminian readers hear confirmation of the public act. Solomon has been seen on the king’s mule, with the same company the narrator has already named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that Jonathan is reporting, not inventing, the procession. The mule and the guard are the visible tokens of David’s appointment.

Both traditions take the verse as a faithful summary of what was done on the way to Gihon, now spoken into Adonijah’s hearing.

verses.text: Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king in Gihon. They have come up from there rejoicing, so that the city rang again. This is the noise that you have heard.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king in Gihon. They have come up from there rejoicing, so that the city rang again. This is the noise that you have heard.” The uproar Joab asked about is explained: it is the sound of that rejoicing.

Arminian readers hear the anointing located and the noise identified. Gihon is the place, and the city itself has rung with the joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let Jonathan close the question of verse 41. The noise is not a riot of unknown origin; it is the sound of Solomon’s anointing coming up from Gihon.

Both traditions read the verse as the public fact now named at the rival feast.

verses.text: Also, Solomon sits on the throne of the kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
He adds, “Also, Solomon sits on the throne of the kingdom.” The appointment has reached the seat itself, not only the spring and the shout.

Arminian readers hear a completed seating. Solomon is not merely acclaimed on the road; he sits on the throne of the kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the short, heavy clause. The throne of the kingdom is already occupied, as David had commanded when he sent them to Gihon.

Both traditions take the sitting as the political fact Adonijah must now face.

verses.text: Moreover the king’s servants came to bless our lord King David, saying, ‘May your God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne;’ and the king bowed himself on the bed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan further reports that the king’s servants came to bless David, saying, “May your God make the name of Solomon better than your name, and make his throne greater than your throne;” and that “the king bowed himself on the bed.” The blessing echoes Benaiah’s prayer, and David, still on his bed, bows.

Arminian readers hear honor given to David even as the greater name is asked for Solomon. The aged king is able to bow and to receive that blessing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the bed. David’s weakness has not kept him from taking part; he bows, and the servants bless him in the terms already heard from Benaiah.

Both traditions take the report as the court’s consent, joined to David’s own gesture of reception.

verses.text: Also thus said the king, ‘Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has given one to sit on my throne today, my eyes even seeing it.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan closes with David’s own words: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has given one to sit on my throne today, my eyes even seeing it.” The speech begun in verse 43 ends here. David blesses the LORD for a successor given today, seen with his own eyes.

Arminian readers hear thanksgiving for a gift actually seen. The LORD has given one to sit on the throne, and David lives to see it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the last word of the report is praise. David does not merely confirm a policy; he blesses the LORD, the God of Israel, for the one given to sit on his throne.

Both traditions receive that blessing as shared ground: the kingdom’s next sitting is confessed as the LORD’s gift, seen in David’s lifetime.

verses.text: All the guests of Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and each man went his way.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the guests of Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and each man went his way. The feast breaks. Fear, not a further council, ends the gathering.

Arminian readers hear a real collapse of support. The guests are free to stay or to go, and they go, each man his own way.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to dress the scene up. Fear rises, the men stand, and the company dissolves.

Both traditions describe the flight as the narrator does, without ridicule and without turning it into a parable.

verses.text: Adonijah was afraid because of Solomon; and he arose, and went, and hung onto the horns of the altar.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adonijah was afraid because of Solomon; and he arose, and went, and hung onto the horns of the altar. The claimant seeks refuge at the altar, as the narrative states, by taking hold of its horns.

Arminian readers take the fear and the flight as his own act. The horns of the altar are a place he goes to in hope of safety; the verse does not pause to legislate the custom, and it should not be turned into a type.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the description spare. Adonijah is afraid because of Solomon, and he hangs onto the horns of the altar.

Both traditions report the appeal for sanctuary as the text gives it, without inventing a legal commentary or a symbolic reading the narrator does not supply.

verses.text: Solomon was told, “Behold, Adonijah fears King Solomon; for, behold, he is hanging onto the horns of the altar, saying, ‘Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not kill his servant with the sword.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon is told that Adonijah fears King Solomon, that he is hanging onto the horns of the altar, and that he is saying, “Let King Solomon swear to me first that he will not kill his servant with the sword.” The request is for an oath, and it is made from the altar.

Arminian readers hear Adonijah asking for a sworn promise before he leaves that place. He names himself Solomon’s servant and asks not to be killed with the sword.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the message reaches Solomon as a plea for an oath, not as a confession already accepted. The horns of the altar and the requested swear are reported together.

Both traditions take the petition as it is worded and wait for Solomon’s reply in the next verse.

verses.text: Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of his shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of his shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness is found in him, he shall die.” The answer is a condition, not an unqualified pardon.

Arminian readers hear a real alternative still open. Clemency is promised if Adonijah shows himself worthy; death is promised if wickedness is found in him. The later request in chapter 2 should be read in light of this condition, not as if this verse had already settled every future act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep both halves of the sentence. “not a hair of his shall fall to the earth” stands only with the “if”, and the second “if” is equally plain.

Both traditions describe this as conditional clemency. It is mercy with a warning, given in Solomon’s own words, without a party dispute over succession ethics.

verses.text: So King Solomon sent, and they brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed down to King Solomon; and Solomon said to him, “Go to your house.”
verses.arminianNotes:
King Solomon sends, and they bring Adonijah down from the altar. He comes and bows down to King Solomon, and Solomon says, “Go to your house.” The unit ends with a dismissal to his house, not with an execution and not with a new office.

Arminian readers hear a present sparing. Adonijah bows, and he is sent home under the condition already spoken, still responsible for what he will do.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same close. He is brought down, he bows, and the king’s word is, “Go to your house.”

Both traditions leave him there, alive under Solomon’s terms. The chapter does not yet tell what he will later ask, and this ending should not be made to say more than it does.
